accepted.title: Persistent focal pain after improvement with rehabilitation

record.title: Persistent focal pain after improvement with rehabilitation
fairness: The best offered answer is elective epigastric hernia assessment. The learner must distinguish the improved broad functional complaint from the persistent focal mechanical pain, then choose a different treatment pathway. This is moderate at the lower end, not a hard item.

The reduction response and painless broad ridge are necessary symptom-localization observations, not pre-answer diagnostic labels. Rehabilitation and observation represent attribution and symptom-significance errors; no option-length, grammatical, absolute or convergence shortcut independently selects the key.
The explanation appropriately recommends assessment rather than promising that an operation will relieve every symptom. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified from the supplied content.

The standalone presentation supplies the earlier rehabilitation and response; no missing preceding node is needed. Name, age, sex, short complaint and complete task are present. This is an offline editorial PASS, not source verification or clinical approval.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old man, returns to clinic after core rehabilitation for a broad midline ridge. His balance has improved, but lifting still produces focal pain above the navel. Standing examination shows fat protruding through a small gap there; pressure returning the fat through the gap stops the pain. The broad ridge itself is painless.
after.Task: Which next plan best addresses {patientName}'s persistent lifting pain?
Options: **KEY:** Refer for elective epigastric hernia repair assessment
Extend the same core rehabilitation programme
Observe the focal defect at routine annual review

accepted.explanation: Two problems can coexist. Improvement in balance does not explain away pain that is reproduced by protrusion through a focal defect and stops with reduction. That persistent mechanical symptom supports elective hernia assessment.

accepted.title: Recurrent deep mesh infection after drainage and directed therapy

record.title: Recurrent deep mesh infection after drainage and directed therapy
fairness: The best offered answer is mesh excision with debridement. Collapsed cavity volume must be distinguished from eradication of a prosthetic infection; recurrent purulence, a tract to retained mesh and the same deep organism then justify changing source-control strategy despite stability.

The favorable mesh material/location and stable physiology make continued salvage a recognizable temptation. The update supplies the important counterevidence. Excision is not selected merely by being the longest or most cautious option, and the repeated retain-mesh component does not converge on the key.

The exact removal extent and reconstruction are appropriately left to the treating team. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the wording does not make a particular antibiotic duration or universal explantation threshold a rule.

The presentation and current update together establish the completed drainage and culture-directed course. The isolated node remains coherent without its former initial-salvage companion or that companion's feedback.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 58-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews his hospital records after his first incisional mesh repair. Drainage had begun recently. At the recorded assessment he was alert, eating and haemodynamically stable. The operative record placed macroporous monofilament polypropylene outside the peritoneal cavity. CT showed a localized fluid cavity around part of that mesh. A deep sample grew bacteria; the skin opening communicated with the cavity. No bowel communication was demonstrated on the completed evaluation.
after.Current update: The drain reached the cavity, the antibiotic course matched the deep culture, and repeat imaging showed that the fluid cavity had collapsed. Purulent drainage nevertheless returned through a tract to the retained mesh. Repeat deep culture grew the same organism. {patientName} remained stable.
after.Task: Which source-control recommendation now best fits {patientName}'s persistent infection?
Options: **KEY:** Excise mesh and debride the repair plane
Retain mesh and repeat drainage with directed antibiotics
Retain mesh and excise the cutaneous sinus tract

accepted.explanation: A collapsed fluid cavity is not the same as eradication of implant infection. The documented drainage and culture-directed course were adequate, yet purulence and the same organism recurred at the retained mesh. Operative excision assessment is appropriate; the exact removal extent and reconstruction plan require the treating team.

accepted.title: Broad functional symptoms with a separate reducible navel defect

record.title: Broad functional symptoms with a separate reducible navel defect
fairness: Initial rehabilitation with observation of the focal defect is the best offered sequence. The resident must distinguish intact broad midline separation from the real focal hernia, attribute the complaint using the different symptom responses, and choose an initial treatment rather than operate on the most visible defect.

The absence of prior rehabilitation establishes treatment stage. All three options contain rehabilitation, so that word does not uniquely identify the key. The symptom responses are necessary localization evidence; removing them would make focal repair more defensible.

Immediate focal repair targets the wrong demonstrated symptom source; immediate plication escalates before a conservative trial. The explanation says rehabilitation can be considered and does not promise efficacy or turn examination support into a validated diagnostic test. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The node stands alone with no dependence on a later symptomatic-hernia case. Patient identity, demographics, complaint and task are complete.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 47-year-old woman, attends clinic because her middle abdomen domes and feels weak when she rises from a chair. Ultrasound during the movement shows the rectus muscles separating across a broad segment while tissue remains continuous between them. A separate small opening at the navel admits fat during straining and empties when she lies down. Pressing the navel and reducing that protrusion do not reproduce or relieve the weakness; supporting the broad midline does. She has not tried supervised rehabilitation.
after.Task: Which initial treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s abdominal-wall findings and functional complaint?
Options: **KEY:** Start core rehabilitation; observe the focal navel defect at follow-up
Repair the focal navel defect; then start core rehabilitation at follow-up
Plicate the broad midline; then start core rehabilitation at follow-up

accepted.explanation: There are two findings: a broad intact but separated midline and a focal reducible opening. The weakness follows the broad segment, not the focal protrusion. Consider rehabilitation first and observe the asymptomatic focal defect. If symptoms instead localized to that opening and improved with reduction, the focal repair pathway would become more appropriate.

accepted.title: Reinforcement after a recognized and controlled enterotomy

record.title: Reinforcement after a recognized and controlled enterotomy
fairness: Permanent macroporous synthetic reinforcement is a defensible best offered answer within the stated selected repair scope. The learner must distinguish a controlled bowel event with feasible closure from an unresolved emergency-abdomen problem, then resist automatically choosing a biologic implant because an enterotomy occurred.

The temporary-coverage alternative represents overreacting to the bowel event; biologic reinforcement is the closer material-selection error. The anatomical and physiological observations make these distinctions possible without a diagnosis label that names the implant.

Source control does not erase the occurrence of contamination. The explanation appropriately restricts its conclusion to the selected single-stage scope and does not recommend a universal emergency mesh plane. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The exact newer guideline recommendation has not been independently verified in this offline review; this editorial PASS does not endorse its evidence mapping or confer clinical approval. Clinician sign-off should retain the conditional scope rather than turn this into a universal synthetic-mesh rule after any enterotomy.
The retrospective operative record is complete enough to stand alone and supplies the mechanism of the bowel injury, current bowel status, closure feasibility and decision stage.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 60-year-old man, attends clinic after discharge while the founder reviews an outside emergency ventral-hernia operation. The trapped bowel regained perfusion after release. During adhesiolysis a full-thickness small-bowel enterotomy was recognized immediately and securely repaired. A limited local spill was removed; repeated inspection found no continuing leak, residual contamination or bowel segment needing reassessment. He was off vasoactive support before and after this event, with maintained perfusion and no ongoing resuscitation requirement. The fascia met with gentle approximation and a closed tissue layer separated bowel from the available reinforcement plane.
after.Task: Which reinforcement strategy best fits {patientName}'s recorded end-of-operation findings?
Options: **KEY:** Complete repair with permanent macroporous synthetic reinforcement
Complete repair with non-cross-linked porcine dermal reinforcement
Defer reinforcement and use temporary abdominal coverage

accepted.explanation: The bowel event is explicitly a repaired enterotomy during adhesiolysis, not an unexplained opening. Interpret its control, the bowel and physiology, and direct closure feasibility before selecting reinforcement. These findings support the selected single-stage scope in which permanent macroporous synthetic mesh is favored. Continuing leakage, uncertain bowel or unresolved physiology would change the decision stage rather than automatically select a biologic implant. No emergency plane ranking is tested.

accepted.title: Improving postoperative fluid pocket with an earlier positive surface swab

record.title: Improving postoperative fluid pocket with an earlier positive surface swab
fairness: Observation with reassessment is the best offered plan. The resident must determine what compartment the positive culture actually sampled, then integrate the improving asymptomatic pocket and healed wound rather than treat the organism name in isolation.

Aspiration for a purported deep infection and cephalexin for a presumed current skin infection are credible errors. The sample location, absent communication and current wound findings resolve them. The statement that the pocket was not sampled is necessary specimen-provenance information, not a reason to remove a safety-critical distinction.

The explanation does not declare every surface swab meaningless, prove sterility or exclude future infection. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified and no unsupported aspiration deadline is taught.
The earlier swab and current improvement have clear chronology. This node stands alone, and its content does not require the separate later symptomatic-seroma case.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old woman, attends clinic three weeks after laparoscopic ventral mesh repair. A painless soft fullness at the old sac is smaller than at the prior visit and does not limit movement. Ultrasound shows simple fluid, an intact repair and no tract to the skin. The incision is now closed without redness, tenderness or drainage; she has no fever. A result posted today reports methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus from a swab rubbed over a shallow skin separation at the earlier visit. The fluid pocket was never sampled.
after.Task: Which management plan best fits {patientName}'s current fluid-pocket course and the newly posted culture result?
Options: **KEY:** Continue observation with a clinic reassessment
Perform sterile image-guided aspiration with culture
Start oral cephalexin with a clinic reassessment

accepted.explanation: Interpret the sample before acting on its organism: a prior surface swab did not sample this fluid. The current shrinking painless pocket and closed noninflamed wound favor observation. This does not prove that superficial swabs are always contamination or exclude future deep infection; new local/systemic findings would require reassessment. No antibiotic dose or aspiration deadline is implied.

accepted.title: Selecting the biopsy target in a multinodular thyroid

record.title: Selecting the biopsy target in a multinodular thyroid
fairness: The learner must rank morphology against size, then select the target. The larger spongiform lesion is a credible size-driven error; observation of both misses the smaller suspicious lesion.

Left-nodule FNA is the best offered plan. A large spongiform nodule can sometimes also be sampled, so the explanation appropriately says it can be observed rather than asserting that sampling it is forbidden. The right-only option leaves the higher-priority lesion unsampled.
No material nonmedical wording shortcut or confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the named patient, age/sex and complete task are coherent.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 55-year-old man, attends clinic after a thyroid ultrasound. TSH is within the laboratory interval. The right lobe contains a 2.7-cm entirely spongiform nodule; the left contains a 1.4-cm solid hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins and punctate echogenic foci. Cervical nodes have preserved morphology.
after.Task: Which thyroid sampling plan should be arranged for {patientName}?
Options: **KEY:** FNA of the left 1.4-cm nodule
FNA of the right 2.7-cm nodule
Ultrasound surveillance of both nodules

accepted.explanation: The smaller left lesion reaches the suspicious-pattern threshold; maximum diameter should not select the right lesion. The right spongiform nodule can be observed; sampling it as the target leaves the more concerning lesion unassessed. The right pattern permits observation, but the left lesion still needs sampling.

record.title: Methimazole adjustment with low free hormones and persistent TSH suppression
fairness: The table creates a genuine conflict: the learner must interpret low free hormones despite suppressed TSH, then reduce synthesis inhibition rather than maintain or increase it. The numerical choices are parallel and do not reveal the key without interpreting the data.

Reducing to 10 mg is the best of the three offered prescriptions. These observations establish dose reduction more securely than they uniquely establish an exact optimal dose; offline review does not independently verify that exact dosing choice. Melissa's exact-version dose review remains necessary.
The later fever/sore-throat event in N11 is a distinct, coherent complication rather than a restatement of this dose-adjustment lesson.
suggestions: Consider trimming the already-managed propranolol narrative. Keep the free-hormone/TSH discordance and explicit dose history, and have the named clinician verify the exact prescription.

accepted.title: Symptom treatment when thyrotoxicosis reflects hormone release

record.title: Symptom treatment when thyrotoxicosis reflects hormone release
fairness: The resident must interpret low uptake with the painless course and relevant exposure history as destructive hormone release, then choose symptom relief rather than synthesis blockade or anti-inflammatory treatment.
Propranolol is the best offered initial medication for this stable symptomatic presentation. Methimazole and prednisone represent plausible mechanism and painful-thyroiditis confusions.
No diagnosis is supplied before the decision, and the short medication labels are parallel. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; no unsupported numerical threshold is needed.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 38-year-old man, attends clinic with palpitations after a painless episode of neck fullness. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. Receptor antibodies are negative and an uptake study shows little thyroid activity. He takes no thyroid hormone and has had no recent iodine-containing treatment or contrast. Pulse is regular and blood pressure is stable.
after.Task: Which initial medication best fits {patientName}’s current thyroid-related symptoms?
Options: **KEY:** Propranolol
Methimazole
Prednisone

accepted.explanation: The low-uptake, antibody-negative painless course supports release of stored hormone; beta-blockade can relieve palpitations while the course is followed. Blocking new synthesis does not treat hormone leakage from destructive thyroiditis. Anti-inflammatory treatment is not the initial choice for this painless stable course; painful inflammatory thyroiditis would be a different setting.

accepted.title: Central-neck management for small bilateral node-negative papillary cancers

record.title: Central-neck management for small bilateral node-negative papillary cancers
fairness: The resident must separate the bilateral intrathyroidal primary burden from the indication for nodal surgery. Bilateral cancers can tempt bilateral clearance, but the small noninvasive cN0 profile supports avoiding routine prophylactic central dissection.

Observation is the best offered central-neck plan. The explanation properly qualifies the recommendation as not routinely requiring prophylactic dissection, rather than claiming that normal imaging excludes microscopic metastases.
The three choices concern the same nodal decision. The later postoperative surveillance event in N14 follows coherently, and this explanation does not give its marker-interpretation answer.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old man, attends clinic before total thyroidectomy for biopsy-confirmed papillary cancers in both lobes, measuring 1.4 and 0.9 cm. Neither lesion extends beyond the thyroid on ultrasound. The central and lateral cervical compartments have been surveyed and no abnormal nodes are seen. There is no clinical distant disease.
after.Task: Which central-neck plan should accompany {patientName}’s planned thyroidectomy?
Options: **KEY:** Observe the central compartments
Dissect the right central compartment
Dissect both central compartments

accepted.explanation: The small noninvasive clinically node-negative papillary cancers do not routinely require prophylactic central dissection. There is no established involved central target or advanced primary here to justify routine prophylactic right dissection. Bilateral thyroid primaries do not automatically establish a need for bilateral prophylactic central dissection in this small noninvasive cN0 profile.

accepted.title: Obtaining representative tissue from a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass

record.title: Obtaining representative tissue from a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass
fairness: The resident must recognize an aggressive unresolved lineage problem, then choose tissue acquisition that can support architecture and ancillary studies before committing to resection. This contrasts meaningfully with the routine first-inadequate-nodule pathway in N03.

Image-guided core biopsy is the best offered plan in this context. An optimized repeat aspirate with appropriate ancillary testing can be useful in selected cases, so the explanation correctly avoids claiming that FNA can never diagnose lymphoma.

The stable airway findings permit diagnostic workup and are decision-critical rather than disposable reassurance. Autoimmune hypothyroidism is a legitimate clinical clue, not a language-only label giveaway. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Consider specifying representative viable tissue and appropriate ancillary specimen handling in post-answer feedback after clinician/source verification. Do not imply that any core containing only necrosis will settle the diagnosis.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old woman with longstanding autoimmune hypothyroidism, attends clinic with a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass. The outside aspirate contains necrosis and mixed atypical cells, insufficient for lineage classification. Cross-sectional imaging shows a thyroid-centered mass but no critical airway narrowing; she has no stridor.
after.Task: Which diagnostic procedure should be arranged next for {patientName}’s thyroid mass?
Options: **KEY:** Ultrasound-guided core biopsy
Repeat thyroid FNA
Diagnostic thyroid lobectomy

accepted.explanation: The aggressive mass and inadequate lineage sample warrant representative tissue that can support architecture and ancillary studies before a definitive operation. Another aspirate may still lack sufficient material for the current aggressive lineage question after necrotic nondiagnostic sampling. Resection before biopsy risks committing to surgery for a process such as lymphoma for which that operation may be inappropriate.

accepted.title: A benign aspirate from a different thyroid target

record.title: A benign aspirate from a different thyroid target
fairness: The defensible best answer is ultrasound-guided right-nodule FNA. The specimen and needle records establish that the benign result concerns the left lesion; the separate right lesion has measured suspicious morphology and sufficient size to support sampling. Neither whole-gland reassurance nor immediate diagnostic lobectomy follows from these findings.

Two consequential interpretations remain: limit the benign result to its actual target, then apply the right lesion's risk features to choose initial tissue assessment. The side labels are necessary provenance, not a key-only wording match; every option concerns the right lesion. This is moderate application of core nodule assessment, not a hard item merely because two nodules are described.
The standalone case supplies the patient's age, sex, short complaint, prior sampling and current findings. No earlier node or explanation is required. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

accepted.title: Cross-sectional mapping when invasive thyroid cancer is suspected

record.title: Cross-sectional mapping when invasive thyroid cancer is suspected
fairness: Neck and mediastinal CT with IV contrast is the defensible best offered study. Retroclavicular nodal disease, the posterior interface, dysphagia and ipsilateral fold immobility establish a reason for cross-sectional operative mapping beyond the completed ultrasound.

The resident must infer possible deep/invasive disease and then weigh useful contrast-enhanced anatomy against a possible later radioiodine course. Noncontrast CT is a credible iodine-avoidance error; the two CT labels are parallel. Mentioning radioiodine introduces a real competing consideration rather than announcing that contrast is permissible.

The known papillary diagnosis appropriately precedes a different management task. Renal function and the absence of an acute airway problem support the proposed elective assessment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; this review does not establish a particular postcontrast radioiodine interval.
This is a complete standalone case. It does not require the earlier mapping or later nodal-surgery task to supply the cancer diagnosis, imaging findings or current decision.

A completed central and lateral ultrasound survey shows confluent right lower-neck nodes extending behind the clavicle and a posterior thyroid margin merging with tissue beside the trachea. after.Task: Which additional imaging plan best supports {patientName}’s operative assessment?

The existing complete survey has identified deep/invasive concerns; repeating the same acoustic approach does not supply the required cross-sectional relationships.

record.title: A fluid-only aspirate from a purely cystic lesion
fairness: Ultrasound observation is the best offered plan. The pre-aspiration images describe a purely cystic lesion, and the current residual cavity is asymptomatic. A Bethesda I label on its fluid does not automatically establish the same repeat-biopsy need as an inadequately sampled solid nodule.

The learner must interpret the relationship between original morphology and specimen contents, then decide whether the usual nondiagnostic-cytology pathway applies. Repeat FNA is a credible overapplication of that pathway; diagnostic lobectomy is premature. This tests a practical exception to a core rule rather than recognition of a supplied benign diagnosis.

The absence of a solid component and pressure symptoms is decision-critical, not gratuitous exclusion of distractors. The case gives the pre- and post-aspiration chronology and stands alone. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The broad observation label does not justify inventing a specific follow-up interval.

fairness: Tumor/cava resection with preservation of kidney and colon is the best offered plan. The morphology, myoid panel, and caval involvement support leiomyosarcoma, while the organ interfaces do not supply an indication to remove either adjacent organ.

The two consequential steps are inferring the tumor family from the biopsy/venous context and applying its operative implications to the actual organ interfaces. The broad kidney-and-colon operation is the closest credible error through overgeneralization of retroperitoneal liposarcoma surgery.

The uninvolved interfaces understandably favor organ preservation, but they are necessary findings rather than disposable answer hints: histotype can affect how apparent interfaces are used in retroperitoneal operative planning. The diagnosis itself is not supplied in the visible pre-answer fields.

All options include tumor/cava removal and balance kidney and colon inclusion. There is no component-frequency convergence. The isolated kidney-only and colon-only additions are weaker distractors than the multivisceral plan, so this is moderate rather than hard.
No definite clinical inaccuracy is identified. Preservation is judged for the stated records, not as a promise that imaging always excludes operative adherence or microscopic invasion.

after.Task: Under the SEOM thymic-tumour guideline, which procedural plan best fits {patientName}'s current work-up?
Options: **KEY:** Complete thymectomy with intact lesion removal
Limited lesion excision with thymus preservation
Percutaneous core biopsy before treatment selection

accepted.explanation: The solid enhancing thymic-bed lesion, preserved tissue planes and lack of separate nodal or pleural disease favor a localized resectable thymic epithelial tumour. These observations do not prove histology, and normal AFP and beta-hCG do not exclude all alternatives. In this high-probability resectable scenario, the SEOM guideline permits upfront surgery without mandatory biopsy and prefers complete thymectomy, including residual thymus and perithymic fat, over mass-only excision. Two consequential distinctions remain: infer adequate oral delivery from the clinical response, then distinguish unfinished treatment from prevention. The balanced four-cell matrix does not select the key by majority-component convergence.

'Scheduled oral medicines taken without vomiting' supports two oral options, while the unfinished virologic course supports two treatment-dose options. The resident interprets the neutrophil trajectory in a multiple-drug setting, then preserves antiviral treatment exposure while addressing another marrow suppressant. Lowering an otherwise appropriate treatment dose or treating active disease with letermovir are not equally supported alternatives.

fields.before: Martin Bell, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after another resolved episode of left-arm weakness yesterday. Four weeks earlier, a similar event led to detection of atrial fibrillation. The initial team favored cardiac embolism and started warfarin. Recorded INRs since then are 2.4, 2.6 and 2.5, with the latest drawn during yesterday's assessment. Brain MRI shows two small recent right cortical infarcts without hemorrhage or edema. CTA shows ordinary 81% right ICA stenosis with a patent normal-caliber distal vessel and a low cervical lesion. He lives independently, walks without angina or dyspnea, and has no prior neck surgery or radiation. The procedural teams meet audited guideline risk criteria. Lipid treatment and the indicated AF prevention continue under the treating teams' perioperative protocol.

claims.limitation: Single adequate current primer; no institutional harm rate or safety-culture score is inferred.
claims.applicablePopulation: Healthcare teams improving clinic, ambulatory-surgery and care-transition processes.

claims.statement: Event reporting is useful when reports lead to further analysis and tracked process improvements.
claims.limitation: No asserted requirement to formally investigate every report; local prioritization is necessary.
claims.applicablePopulation: Healthcare teams improving clinic, ambulatory-surgery and care-transition processes.

claims.statement: Noncontrast CT can resolve ureteral stone location and obstruction after an inconclusive ultrasound in a stable nonpregnant adult.
claims.limitation: Scoped escalation, not a universal first test; a different clinical syndrome or pregnancy changes imaging selection.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Pain resolution or reported passage does not reliably confirm ureteral stone clearance; follow-up imaging can establish passage.
claims.limitation: Single specialty guideline; modality and interval depend on the original stone and patient. No exact follow-up interval is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Active liver disease is a contraindication to systemic methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy.
claims.limitation: Specific liver disease is supplied; no invented enzyme threshold or dose. Surgery is assessed with persistent symptoms and a confirmed ectopic, not from a single hCG result.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: New or persistent unilateral pain during an unlocated pregnancy requires prompt pregnancy-capable reassessment despite initially normal vital signs.
claims.limitation: The exact specialist pathway depends on local resources; escalating hemorrhage requires emergency care, not a routine test wait.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: A confirmed intrauterine pregnancy does not eliminate the need to evaluate the adnexa when heterotopic pregnancy is clinically plausible.
claims.limitation: No numerical assisted-conception risk or treatment ranking is asserted.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Transvaginal ultrasound is an appropriate localization study in a symptomatic early pregnancy when prior transabdominal views do not resolve the adnexa.
claims.limitation: Declined/unacceptable transvaginal acquisition requires a different plan; no claim of superiority over appendiceal MRI for every RLQ presentation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Detectable hCG and an empty uterine cavity do not by themselves locate a pregnancy or prove completed miscarriage.
claims.limitation: No discriminatory hCG value, serial-rise cutoff or viability diagnosis is taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: An obstructed collecting system with convincing systemic infection needs prompt upper-tract drainage plus antimicrobial and resuscitative care.
claims.limitation: Single specialty guideline. A nephrostomy or ureteral stent can provide drainage; neither is universally preferred. Fever/rigors, bacteriuria and obstruction are supplied rather than sterile pyuria alone.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Definitive stone treatment follows drainage and adequate treatment of the accompanying infection.
claims.limitation: Single specialty guideline; no fixed waiting period or universal preferred definitive procedure. Stenting relieves obstruction without proving stone clearance.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: When stone treatment is chosen and interrupting necessary anticoagulation poses excessive risk, retrograde ureteroscopy can be considered; shock-wave and antegrade treatment are unsuitable under uncorrected anticoagulation/coagulopathy.
claims.limitation: Single specialty guideline; clinician-led procedure and anticoagulation decisions are required. No drug dose, bridging instruction or universal timing of intervention is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the exact constructed specimen or procedural constraints.

claims.statement: High drain-fluid creatinine relative to serum after pelvic surgery supports concern for a urinary leak.
claims.limitation: Single surgical guideline. No diagnostic ratio cutoff is asserted and this finding does not locate the defect.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Nephrographic and excretory CT urography evaluates a suspected postoperative ureteral injury.
claims.limitation: Single surgical guideline. An unperformed excretory acquisition is distinct from a missing exported series; renal impairment/contrast constraints must be considered.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Retrograde filling cystography evaluates bladder leakage; passive excreted contrast in an underfilled bladder is not an equivalent examination.
claims.limitation: Single guideline. No exact instillation volume is prescribed in this packet; adequate retrograde distension is specified.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: A bladder scan measures retained bladder urine; a prevoid volume does not establish the postvoid residual.
claims.limitation: The current government source confirms residual assessment; the local URECA claim was verified 2026-09-17 and is not freshly re-retrieved. No universal numeric threshold is asserted.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Preserved arterial Doppler flow does not exclude torsion when the clinical course and ovarian morphology remain concerning.
claims.limitation: Single contemporary society recommendation. The case uses a text report, not a claim that the learner viewed an unavailable scan.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: A clinically concerning adnexal torsion presentation requires urgent gynecologic operative evaluation.
claims.limitation: Single contemporary society recommendation. No viability cutoff, image-based ovarian removal rule or fixed time window is taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults within the stated constructed case constraints.

claims.statement: Unilateral ovarian enlargement with stromal edema and peripheral follicles can accompany adnexal torsion.
claims.limitation: Morphology and symptoms are interpreted together; no individual feature or size cutoff establishes the diagnosis.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated constructed clinical findings.

claims.statement: NASCET diameter reduction uses the narrowest residual lumen relative to a normal distal internal-carotid lumen.
claims.limitation: The estimated original bulb diameter belongs to a different method; distal collapse invalidates ordinary grading.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: Routine carotid intervention is not recommended for ordinary symptomatic carotid stenosis below 50%.
claims.limitation: ESO directly supports the CEA boundary; ESVS supports the broader intervention boundary. Recurrent events despite prevention require a separate evaluation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: Carotid intervention supplements continued vascular risk reduction and antiplatelet treatment.
claims.limitation: No exact drug dose or individualized perioperative antiplatelet protocol is inferred.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: Suitable adults with recent ipsilateral symptoms and 70-99% carotid stenosis benefit from CEA with medical prevention.
claims.limitation: Excludes distal collapse, occlusion, major infarction and unsuitable operative risk. The exact severe range is directly supported.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: CAS can be considered when carotid surgery is unsuitable for technical, anatomic or medical reasons.
claims.limitation: A case-specific alternative, not a rule that every prior neck operation or radiation exposure mandates stenting.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: Established atherosclerotic ICA occlusion is outside ordinary stenosis indications for CEA or CAS.
claims.limitation: One checked guideline; excludes acute salvage thrombosis and investigational recanalization. Distal collateral filling does not demonstrate a patent cervical lumen.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: EC-IC bypass is not recommended for stroke prevention in atherosclerotic extracranial ICA occlusion.
claims.limitation: One guideline directly checked; not a rule for moyamoya or other bypass indications.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: Severe narrowing accompanied by a reduced distal ICA caliber requires assessment for near-occlusion rather than routine percent grading.
claims.limitation: One direct guideline. Definitive interpretation uses the whole angiographic anatomy, not a solitary small measurement.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: ESVS advises against routine CEA or CAS for near-occlusion with distal collapse when symptoms have not recurred on medical treatment.
claims.limitation: Limited evidence and guideline uncertainty: ESO makes no clear recommendation. Recurrent symptoms despite medical treatment require a separate multidisciplinary decision; that branch remains unkeyed.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: For appropriate stable symptomatic patients, CEA is favored early, ideally within two weeks of the last retinal or cerebral event.
claims.limitation: Does not mandate emergency surgery immediately after a large stroke or apply to thrombolysis without separate assessment.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: An INR of 2.0-3.0 is the usual warfarin therapeutic range for secondary stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.
claims.limitation: One directly checked guideline. Fictional serial INR observations establish the case context and are not a general claim of perfect adherence or complete time-in-range.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: ESVS recommends carotid revascularization for recurrent events in the territory of a 50-99% stenosis during therapeutic anticoagulation after an initial cardiac attribution.
claims.limitation: The exact intervention recommendation is ESVS recommendation 64, consensus level C. Canadian guidance independently supports checking other causes of stroke during anticoagulation. Both the intervention indication and procedure route need clinical review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: A recent retinal event belongs to the carotid on the same side; hemispheric symptoms require localization before attributing a carotid lesion.
claims.limitation: Attribution still requires exclusion of competing causes; stenosis size alone is insufficient.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: In operable symptomatic patients older than 70, CEA generally has a preferable procedural stroke-risk profile to transfemoral CAS.
claims.limitation: Applies to transfemoral evidence; does not establish TCAR superiority or prohibit stenting in every older patient.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: Symptomatic carotid intervention selection includes the treating team's audited procedural outcomes.
claims.limitation: Drafts stipulate that both teams satisfy the applicable guideline criterion; no fictional event probability or universal procedure ranking is introduced.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with extracranial atherosclerotic carotid disease in the stated care phase; fictional observations are not empirical thresholds.

claims.statement: Abdominopelvic CT is appropriate to confirm a first suspected diverticulitis presentation and assess its extent or competing diagnoses.
claims.limitation: The first-presentation construct is retained. CT is not required for every already-established recurrence.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated diverticular disease or lower-GI hemorrhage care phase and constraints.

claims.statement: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT is the standard initial cross-sectional study for suspected diverticulitis when the clinical assessment supports its use.
claims.limitation: This ranks the proposed protocol for the constructed bowel-focused problem. Noncontrast CT can still demonstrate diverticulitis and is not characterized as universally incapable of doing so.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated diagnostic or treatment context and the explicitly described counterfactual.

claims.statement: Pneumaturia or fecaluria and bladder gas without recent instrumentation can raise concern for a colonic communication in diverticular disease.
claims.limitation: Single current guideline. Bladder gas has competing causes, so the constructed CT also describes a tract to an adjacent inflamed sigmoid segment.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated diverticular disease or lower-GI hemorrhage care phase and constraints.

claims.statement: Cystoscopy directly inspects the bladder and urethral lumen.
claims.limitation: It does not supply the same extraluminal assessment as pelvic CT. The node tests initial bowel/pelvic imaging, with no bladder-cancer staging objective.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated diagnostic or treatment context and the explicitly described counterfactual.

claims.statement: After recovery from diverticulitis, a patient without a current adequate colorectal examination may need colonoscopy to assess an alternative lesion.
claims.limitation: The authored recovered-abscess patient has no prior complete examination. ACG and ASCRS 2026 differ in how broadly they phrase follow-up after complicated disease, so no blanket repeat rule after a recent adequate examination is keyed.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated diverticular disease or lower-GI hemorrhage care phase and constraints.

claims.statement: Noncontrast CT commonly evaluates urinary stones, and flank or groin pain with hematuria can support that competing pathway.
claims.limitation: Government information supports basic stone imaging and symptoms. It does not exclude stones when hematuria is absent.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated diagnostic or treatment context and the explicitly described counterfactual.

claims.statement: Persistent atypical symptoms or concerning residual colonic findings after apparent diverticulitis warrant colonoscopic assessment despite a prior screening examination.
claims.limitation: The scope is evaluation after recovery. This does not claim that superficial negative biopsies exclude an unsampled malignancy.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated diverticular disease or lower-GI hemorrhage care phase and constraints.

claims.statement: Worsening clinical infection with inadequate nonoperative source control supports operative management of diverticulitis.
claims.limitation: Decisions depend on trajectory, drain access and examination. No invented elapsed-time deadline is used.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated diverticular disease or lower-GI hemorrhage care phase and constraints.

claims.statement: CT colonography provides structural colonic images but cannot obtain tissue; an abnormal finding may require a subsequent optical colonoscopy.
claims.limitation: Capability contrast, not a claim that CT colonography is inappropriate in every symptomatic patient. Optical feasibility and the diagnostic question matter.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated diagnostic or treatment context; constructed observations create no new clinical threshold.

claims.statement: Optical colonoscopy directly examines colonic mucosa and can obtain biopsy samples from abnormal tissue.
claims.limitation: Basic capability claim only. The need for the examination and its clinical timing come from separate disease-specific guidance.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated diagnostic or treatment context; constructed observations create no new clinical threshold.

claims.statement: Heller myotomy can be considered before esophagectomy after failed dilation and POEM when anatomy is favorable and prior myotomy is incomplete.
claims.limitation: Exact ACG sequencing rests on small heterogeneous case series. Seoul supports salvage possibilities without a universal ranking.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG recommendation 19 and Seoul recurrence section

claims.statement: Fit patients with severe distortion, disabling retention and prior-treatment failure may require high-volume-center esophagectomy assessment.
claims.limitation: Comprehensive individualized assessment remains necessary. No diameter mandates resection.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG end-stage/recommendation 19 discussion and Seoul esophagectomy section

claims.statement: Adding fundoplication to Heller myotomy reduces distal acid exposure, and a partial wrap is an accepted adjunct.
claims.limitation: Dor and Toupet remain accepted. These two partial wraps are not compared in the candidate.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.

claims.statement: Botulinum toxin is an accepted initial symptom-relief option when achalasia patients cannot undergo definitive junction therapies.
claims.limitation: Benefit is often temporary. Selection depends on procedural and rescue risk.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.

claims.statement: A standardized upright timed barium examination assesses esophageal clearance.
claims.limitation: Individual series are constructed and interpreted with symptoms and anatomy.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG physiology key concepts and Seoul statement 7

claims.statement: Recurrent symptoms after myotomy can arise from residual obstruction, altered anatomy, reflux injury or persistent motor dysfunction.
claims.limitation: One directly checked guideline. Symptoms do not establish which mechanism is active.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.

claims.statement: Expert-confirmed indefinite dysplasia with active inflammation calls for optimized acid suppression and repeat endoscopic sampling before eradication treatment.
claims.limitation: No exact drug dose, timing interval or persistent-IND schedule is authored. Persistent-IND follow-up remains a clinician/source hold.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG surveillance Table 5 and IND discussion.

claims.statement: Established nondysplastic Barrett in a treatment-suitable patient is generally managed with endoscopic surveillance.
claims.limitation: Conditional recommendation. No fixed interval, survival benefit guarantee or lifelong mandate is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.

claims.statement: Confirmed high-grade Barrett dysplasia after careful lesion assessment is an indication for endoscopic eradication therapy rather than routine surveillance.
claims.limitation: Same-society cross-check only; not independent evidence. Esophagectomy may be appropriate for invasive/high-risk disease outside this specific flat-HGD context.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.
claims.verificationLocator: Current ACG recommendation 17 and historical recommendation 30.

claims.statement: For expert-confirmed Barrett indefinite dysplasia with active inflammation during once-daily PPI treatment, increasing PPI frequency to twice daily precedes repeat endoscopic biopsy assessment.
claims.limitation: One adequate detailed guideline. No milligram dose, repeat interval or persistent-indefinite surveillance schedule is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adult Barrett indefinite dysplasia confirmed by expert pathology, with active inflammation during once-daily acid suppression.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG Barrett 2022, Table 5 and indefinite-dysplasia discussion; exact frequency checked from the original guideline PDF hosted by the Portuguese gastroenterology society.

claims.statement: Conventional omeprazole administration can use a dose before breakfast for once-daily therapy and doses before breakfast and dinner for twice-daily therapy.
claims.limitation: No milligram dose or exact minute lead time is authored. Omeprazole is a named example, not a claim of superiority over another PPI. The current patient regimen and adherence are constructed observations.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults using conventional oral PPI therapy; exact cases retain their original eligibility constraints.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG GERD 2022, PPI pharmacology and Optimization of PPI Therapy sections.

claims.statement: Persistent symptoms despite optimized twice-daily PPI in established GERD are evaluated with impedance-pH monitoring on treatment.
claims.limitation: Conditional/low-certainty strategy; timing and adherence must be verified. pH alone does not detect all nonacid events.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG refractory-GERD recommendation 3; Lyon proven-GERD section.

claims.statement: Invasive reflux treatment requires objective reflux evidence; normal endoscopy with unproven GERD calls for off-therapy ambulatory monitoring.
claims.limitation: Guidelines agree on unproven disease; this is not the testing strategy for persistent symptoms in proven GERD.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG refractory-GERD recommendations 2-3; SAGES KQ1 preoperative evaluation.

claims.statement: Preprocedural high-resolution manometry checks for achalasia and absent contractility; normal swallowing or barium transit does not replace it.
claims.limitation: Does not prove reflux or select an operation by itself. Standalone motor-disorder diagnosis belongs to the adjacent topic.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG surgical/endoscopic key concepts; SAGES KQ1.

claims.statement: A commonly used refractory-GERD definition requires persistent symptoms despite an 8-week course of twice-daily PPI; correct administration must also be checked.
claims.limitation: One adequate guideline; this is a commonly used definition, not a universal biological cutoff or prescribed medication dose. The exact course in the case is a constructed observation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with persistent typical symptoms during GERD evaluation.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG 2022 refractory-GERD discussion, definition and Optimization of PPI Therapy; omeprazole optimization trial discussed.

claims.statement: After resection of Barrett-related HGD or selected intramucosal carcinoma, ablation of remaining Barrett mucosa reduces metachronous neoplasia risk.
claims.limitation: The constructed case has favorable mucosal pathology and complete lesion resection. Positive deep margin, submucosal invasion or lymphovascular invasion needs separate management.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.
claims.verificationLocator: Current ACG paragraph after endoscopic-resection discussion; historical recommendation 28.

claims.statement: A visible Barrett lesion requires endoscopic resection for tissue staging before segment ablation.
claims.limitation: Resection method depends on morphology and expertise. No unsupported EMR-versus-ESD ranking is authored; EUS does not replace resection histology for superficial lesions.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults evaluated in a foregut clinic; constructed record details define each narrower population.

claims.statement: After adequate source control of a complicated intra-abdominal infection, a four-day fixed antimicrobial course is supported for the specified improving adult.
claims.limitation: The two consensus statements overlap in authorship. Excludes uncontrolled infection, another antibiotic indication, bacteremia requiring separate management and invasive candidiasis. A drain does not establish persistent infection.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.
claims.verificationLocator: GAIS statement 8 and Italian council recommendation 11

claims.statement: Source control must address the actual infected compartment and ongoing contamination. Drain output from one space does not establish control of a separate collection.
claims.limitation: Compartment comparison is an original application of source-control principles. The two statements share authors and do not count as fully independent corroboration.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.

claims.statement: Continuing or recurrent abdominal infection after source-control treatment requires reassessment for an uncontrolled focus and microbiological mismatch.
claims.limitation: No exact waiting interval is prescribed in the drafts. Sources share some authors. Acute deterioration requires immediate clinical reassessment.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.
claims.verificationLocator: GAIS statements 8-10 and Italian council treatment-duration discussion

claims.statement: Longstanding abdominal drains and collection systems can become colonized, so their culture results may misrepresent organisms causing an active intra-abdominal infection.
claims.limitation: Focused narrative review with limited direct outcome evidence. A positive drain result must be integrated with the current clinical course.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.
claims.verificationLocator: Clinical data and clinical implications sections

claims.statement: Superficial incisional infection involves skin/subcutaneous tissue. Fascia and muscle belong to the deep incisional compartment. Organ-space infection is deeper than these incisional tissues.
claims.limitation: One directly checked publication supports this atom. Additional independent confirmation remains for clinical review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.

claims.statement: Selected postoperative localized abdominal abscesses without generalized peritonitis can receive antibiotics with image-guided drainage when anatomy permits effective access.
claims.limitation: Direct postoperative recommendation is older and low certainty. Current general source-control guidance corroborates it. This atom does not rank diversion/resection techniques for an ongoing enteric leak.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.
claims.verificationLocator: WSES postoperative peritonitis section, recommendation 2C. GAIS source-control section.

claims.statement: Generalized postoperative peritoneal contamination requires prompt operative source-control assessment after initial stabilization.
claims.limitation: The operation is individualized. No reconstruction or stoma choice is scored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.
claims.verificationLocator: WSES postoperative peritonitis and GAIS source-control sections
